sn47.1:1.1: The Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta lacks a detailed set of meditation practices such as those found in the great meditation compilations the Satipaṭṭhānasutta ([mn10](),[dn22]()) and the Kāyagatāsatisutta ([mn119]()). It offers instead a range of contexts and illustrations broadening our understanding of mindfulness.
sn47.1:1.2: Ambapālī was a courtesan who offered this land to the Saṅgha. She later went forth as a *bhikkhunī*; her verses are at [thig13.1](). This seems to be presented as an excerpt from the Mahāparinibbānasutta narrative when the Buddha was staying at her place, but, unlike the next Sutta, it is not, in fact, found there.
sn47.1:2.1: See [sn47.18]() for notes on _ekāyana_. | A _ñāya_ is a “system”, method, or way of practice that proceeds in line with cause and effect. It refers to the pattern of the Buddha’s teaching, especially dependent origination ([sn12.41:12.1](), [an10.92:6.1](); see too [an4.35:3.5]()).
sn47.1:2.3: The idiom _kāye kāyānupassī_, literally “one who observes a body in the body” refers to focusing on a specific aspect of embodied experience, such as the breath, the postures, etc. | “Keen” (or “ardent”, _ātāpī_) implies effort, while “aware” (_sampajāno_) is the wisdom of understanding situation and context. | “Covetousness and displeasure” (_abhijjhādomanassaṁ_) are the strong forms of desire and aversion that are overcome by sense restraint in preparation for meditation.
sn47.1:2.4: “Feelings” (_vedanā_) are the basic tones of pleasant, painful, or neutral, not the complexes we call “emotions”.
sn47.1:2.5: “Mind” (_citta_) is simple awareness. In meditation contexts, “mind” is often similar in meaning to _samādhi_.
sn47.1:2.6: “Principles” (_dhammā_) are the natural “systems” of cause and effect that underlie the “teachings”. The renderings “mind objects” or “mental qualities” are incorrect, as many of the things spoken of in this section are neither mind objects nor mental qualities. “Phenomena” is a possible translation, but the emphasis is not on the “appearance” of things, but on the “principles” governing their conditional relations.
